title: The one you bless
hook: only the one You bless receives this gift (Anand, early pauris)

segments.voice: Yesterday, giaan anjan, and your line, real joy. Today, back to a line from pauri three that was saved for now.

An arcade claw machine. A glass box full of stuffed toys, a metal claw on a joystick. You drop in your coins, steer, line it up perfectly, press the button. The claw closes, lifts, and the toy slips out of its grip, every single time. Then there's the other way to get a toy. Someone who loves you reaches into a bag and simply hands you one. No skill, no coins. You just hold out your hand. Anand Sahib describes the other way.
screen: `A CLAW MACHINE: GRAB, SLIP, AGAIN.` → `OR SOMEONE SIMPLY HANDS IT TO YOU.` → `A LOT OF LIFE FEELS LIKE THE CLAW.`

segments.voice: Back in pauri three, after asking what isn't in the Master's house, the next line says: ghar ta terai sabh kichh hai, jis deh su paavae. Everything is in your house; the one you give it to, receives. That's the claw machine turned upside down. The house is full, but nobody breaks in. It's given. This runs straight through Sikh teaching. Guru Nanak puts it in the Japji, in paraphrase: by our actions we get this body, this garment, but by grace the door of liberation opens. The word there is nadar, the glance of grace, the Master's look of favor, and it's all over the Guru Granth Sahib. Anand keeps returning to it too: bliss is known when the Beloved shows grace. A fair question: does effort still matter? Sikhs would say firmly yes. The same Gurus taught kirat karni, honest work, and seva, service, and daily simran. A Sikh is expected to do the work. But the work isn't a coin in a slot that buys God. It's more like holding your hands out, ready, and the gift still comes as a gift. That changes how it feels to receive. If you grabbed it, you grip it tight, afraid of losing it, a little proud you won. If it was given, you can hold it open-handed, grateful, and share it. You met that posture on day three hundred sixty-two, with karah prasad in cupped hands. Same idea, now in Anand.
screen: `JIS DEH SU PAAVAE.` · `NADAR: THE GLANCE OF GRACE.` · `EFFORT STILL MATTERS.` · `HELD OPEN-HANDED, NOT GRIPPED.` · then, large: `GIVEN, NOT GRABBED.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing in your life that, honestly, you didn't earn: the family you were born into, a teacher who saw something in you, a chance meeting that changed things. Hold it, and notice how differently it sits once you admit it was given. If you pray, you can thank the Giver simply, with Waheguru; if not, just let yourself feel thankful.
Nadar, the glance of grace. Jis deh su paavae: the Master's house holds everything, and the one it's given to receives it, by nadar, not by grabbing.
Your line: given, not grabbed. Open hands can hold what a claw keeps dropping. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within the third pauri of the short Anand Sahib at the close of services; grace, nadar, is a central theme of Sikh scripture alongside honest work, service and remembrance.

chat.says: If grace is a gift, why do Sikhs bother working so hard at prayer and service?
options: Effort matters, like hands held out ready, but nadar, grace, still comes as a gift.
They work to earn grace: do enough service, and God has to pay them back for it.
They don't need to; grace is a gift, so honest work and prayer don't count at all.
chat.meaning: Jis deh su paavae: the one you give to, receives. Sikhs are expected to work, but grace, nadar, comes as a gift, not a purchase.
